text: ABSTRACT
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > ABSTRACT

text: A nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound N-(3-(5-Mercapto-1H-tetrazol-1-yl) phenyl) acetamide (named L) was investigated as a new leveler to develop the microvias Cu fi lling with or without cracked plating in blind via. The synergistic effects of L with other plating additives were investigated by galvanostatic measurements (GMs) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements. The GMs show that the Δη values (Potential difference at different speeds of Cu rotating disk electrode) are approximately 24 mV which usually suggests better Cu fi lling performance for the corresponding electrolyte additives. In addition, the optical microscope (OM) measurements indicated that microvias cracked plating was more likely to occur when there is no accelerator in the copper plating solution. The results of OM experiments also show that the microvia super- fi lling would not appear although the copper plating rate at the bottom of the blind hole is higher than that of the outer copper layer of the blind hole if there is no air agitation in the copper plating solution.

text: 1. Introduction
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 1. Introduction

text: Over recent years, the nano or micro-scale blind vias copper fi lling by electroplating has become one of the most practical methods for the fabrication of integrated circuit packaging substrates and circuit boards (PCBs) [1–6]. To achieve high-reliability interconnection by Cu fi lling blind holes between layers of electronic products is a long term and formidable task with high-density interconnection (HDI) technology. The super fi lling of blind holes is commonly regarded as an ef fi cient way and high performance with no void or seam during the microvia metallization process [7–8]. The super fi lling mode means the electrocrystallization rate speed of copper at the bottom of the blind via is much faster than that at the surface of the PCBs so called bottom-up deposition [9–10]. However, cracked plating that grows from the side and bottom of the blind hole penetrates the copper layer at the corners of the blind holes. It is often found as a serious fault in PCB industrial production, as shown in Fig. 1.
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 1. Introduction

text: Cracked plating is an important reliability failure type of copper electroplating. It is manifested as copper cohesive cracks appearing at the corner locations of the microvias and will result in failures in electric and heat conductivity. The greater harm of the cracked plating phenomenon lies in its concealment. The conductivity of the copper layer for PCBs with cracked plating is usually the same as that of a normal printed circuit board at the early stages, so it is dif fi cult to be detected in electrical testing. However, some problems such as signal interruption and the sudden crash will occur and cause huge economic losses when the electronic devices and products smooth running for a period of time. Hence, there are urgent demands for developing processing guidelines for cracked plating that will lead to stable electroplating structures.
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 1. Introduction

text: In order to ensure product quali fi ed reliability, many chemical additives have been applied in super fi lling process, including an accelerator (bis(3-sulfopropyl) disul fi de, SPS), a suppressor (polyethylene glycol, PEG or PEP(propylene oxide-ethylene oxide-propylene oxide)), and a leveler (Janus Green B, JGB) [11–15]. Among them, leveler ha important effects with regard to the asymmetric electroplating due to its capability of adsorbing at a high electric fi eld for the cathode sur face, which increase the overpotential of copper deposition and strongly inhibits copper deposition in high current density regions [16–18]. According to the literature [19,20], commonly used levelers for copper electroplating are organic compounds and their derivatives such as quaternary ammonium surfactants, dyestuff substances, nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds, and many others. The widely used levelers such as JGB, tricyclazole (TCA), 2-Mercaptopyridine, and 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole (AMBT) play an essential role in greatly hindering the deposition of Cu ion and smooth the surface of the deposited copper fi lm [21–28].

text: 2.2. The Q/Q_O values and PEP concentrations dependence
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 2.2. The Q/Q_O values and PEP concentrations dependence

text: Fig. 5a shows the CV experiment with different concentrations of PEP in the electroplating solution. The strength of suppression of PEP could be evaluated by the integrated area value Q in VAS with a constant concentration of other electroplating additives. Fig. 5b showed the piecewise linear fi tting result of the integrated area value Q/Q_0 of the anode copper dissolution peak. Generally, the smaller Q/ Q_0 value means the higher suppression intensity of copper ion deposition. Fig. 5b shows that the Q/Q_0 value decreases dramatically fi rst and then evolves toward an approximate steady-going value with the PEP increased. Thus, the change rate of Q/Q_0 is divided into two areas, including the linear increase area (PEP concentration less than 10 ppm) and the stable area (PEP concentration greater than 20 ppm). In fact, a critical transition point of Cu stripping peaks occurred when the suppressor concentration was 9.61 ppm, as shown in Fig. 5b. In other words, the 9.61 ppm PEP were adequate to achieve the critical adsorption on the cathode when assumed PEP molecules only constitute a monolayer [32].

text: 2.3. The Q/Q_O values and SPS concentrations dependence
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 2.3. The Q/Q_O values and SPS concentrations dependence

text: The CV measured in the electroplating solution with different concentrations of SPS is shown in Fig. 6. It is usually believed that PEP has a small diffusion coef fi cient in VAS, but it can quickly adsorb adsorbed on the Cu surface through the cooperation of Cl − [33]. On the contrary, SPS has a large diffusion coef fi cient and it is strongly adsorbed on active sites in weak convection conditions [34]. The adsorption of SPS on the electrode surface promotes the reduction of copper ions on the cathode surface and accelerates the Cu deposition rate [35]. The peak current and the Q/Q_0 values of anode copper dissolution gradually increase with increasing SPS, as shown in Fig. 6a and b, respectively. The experimental results showed that the copper dissolution became more and more serious with the increase in SPS concen tration. Taking this Δ n value larger means a good fi lling performance, the GMs measured in the electroplating solution with different concentrations of SPS at two different spinning speeds are shown in Fig. 7. So, the optimal SPS was 6 ppm and Δη is equal to 24 mV when the electroplating bath system contains VAS, 200 ppm PEP, 10 ppm L.

text: A new nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound N-(3-(5-Mercapto-1H-tetrazol-1-yl) phenyl) acetamide was found as a leveler for microvias fi lling in HDI board. The Δ G _ads ^0 shown that the L adsorption on the Cu surface was associated with mainly chemical adsorption processes. The optical microscope measurements indicated that the cracked plating was more likely to occur in a diagonal line across the bottom of the microvia at the corners of the blind holes when there is no accelerator in the copper plating solution. The thickness of deposited copper for the bottom of the microvia was larger than the outside without stirring, and this association may be attributed to PEP concentration non-uniform distribution on the sides and bottom of the microvia. Chronoamperometry tests indicate that the Cu electrodeposition nucleation could be considered as an instantaneous mechanism for the initial few seconds. An optimal copper plating solution composed of the virgin acid solution (VAS) only added the PEP, L, and SPS was found and applied to carry out super fi lling of microvias.

text: 4.1. Electrochemical details
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 4.1. Electrochemical details

text: The electrochemical measurements were carried out with an elec trochemical workstation CHI 760E(Auto-Lab) equipped a standard three-electrode cell containing 250 mL electrolyte. A platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) with a diameter of 5 mm was used as the work ing electrode (WE). The counter electrode (CE) was a copper bar placed in a hollow glass pipe fi lled with base electrolyte. Moreover, the reference electrode (RE) used the mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE). All the potential values involved in this work are referred to SMSE scale. The galvanostatic measurements (GM) were used to investigate the adsorption of additives and evaluate the fi lling ability of the plating solution. Before GM tests, a layer of copper with the thickness of about 500 nm was pre-plated on the platinum rotating disk electrode for 5 min to transform Pt-RDE into Cu-RDE. During the galvanostatic measurements, the spinning speeds of the WE were taken at 100 and 1000 rpm to simulate the bottom and surface of the microvias, respectively. The electrolyte was controlled at a constant temperature of 298 K and the current density was 2.0 \A/dm2.
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 4.1. Electrochemical details

text: The inhibiting effect of copper plating was analyzed by cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests with a rotation speed of 1000 rpm. CV tests were conducted with the Pt-RDE as a working electrode and the scan rate is 5 mV/s while the frequency range is from 0.3 V to − 0.8 V. Chronoamperometry (CA) tests were conducted by the glassy carbon working electrode for a 3 mm diameter. All the experiments mentioned above must be carried out three times under the same conditions to ensure good repeatability.

text: 4.2. Microvia copper electroplating
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 4.2. Microvia copper electroplating

text: Electroplating experiments were performed in a 1500 mL Harring cell. The PCBs fragments by CO _2 laser ablation were used as a tested board for microvia fi lling experiments. The dimensions of the tested board with many microvias were 50 mm * 150 mm. The diameter and depth of the blind microvias were 0.13 mm and 0.08 mm, respectively. Two parallel phosphorus-containing copper boards were used as the anode with the size of 5 cm * 15 cm and placed at a distance of 20 cm in the Harring cell. To ensure better conductivity between the plated copper and the inner copper, smear of the microvias on the tested board were cleaned through a desmear process before the plating. The electroplating test was carried out at a room temperature of 298 K and the current density was kept at 2.0 A/dm2 for 45 min. To enhance the mixing of the plating solution and good mass transfer, continuously fl owing air bubbles were applied to constantly agitate the plating solution throughout the whole electroplating process.
section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 4.2. Microvia copper electroplating

text: In the electroplating process, the virgin acid solution (VAS) included 0.88 M CuSO4 and 0.54 MH_2S0_4.. Formulas of plating baths are C l ^- from NaCl, PEP with a molecular weight of 2650 (BASF) employed as a suppressor, SPS used as an accelerator and L as studied leveler. The fi lling performance of microvias were observed by the cross-sections images using optical microscopy (OM). SEM pictures of the Cu electroplating surface were tested using a high vacuum at 15 keV by the Hitachi SU3500 SEM instrument.
